blocks.text: HTTPS is an aggregate of HTTP and the Secure Sockets Layer (SSL)/Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, wherein the authentication and encryption capabilities of SSL/TLS protect HTTP communications. This is vital because the information that you send on the internet is passed along from one device to another before it reaches the destination server. Therefore, sensitive information, such as credit card numbers, usernames, and passwords might be seen by intermediate devices if the information is sent in clear text over HTTP. When the information is encrypted and protected by the SSL/TLS protocol, only the intended recipient can read the information. To learn more about SSL/TLS, see Understanding SSL/TLS.
Unfortunately, the security provided by SSL/TLS is also being misused in a number of ways:

blocks.item: SSL/TLS encryption is used to hide dangerous content such as viruses, spyware, and other malware.
Attackers build their own websites with SSL/TLS encryption.
Attackers inject their malicious content into well-known and trusted SSL/TLS-enabled sites.
SSL/TLS can be used to hide data leakage; for example, the transmission of sensitive financial documents from an organization.
SSL/TLS can be used to hide the browsing of websites that belong to legal-liability classes.

blocks.text: As more and more websites use HTTPS, including social media such as Facebook and X, the ability to control and inspect traffic to and from these sites has become an important piece of the security posture of an organization.

The Zscaler service can inspect HTTPS traffic from your organization. The service can scan data transactions and apply policies to it. It functions as a full SSL/TLS proxy, or SSL/TLS man-in-the-middle (MITM) proxy.
The Zscaler service does not support SSL/TLS inspection websites that mandate Mutual TLS.

When you enable SSL/TLS Inspection, the Zscaler service establishes a separate SSL/TLS tunnel with the user’s browser and with the destination server. The diagram below shows the Zscaler SSL/TLS Inspection process:

blocks.item: A user opens a browser and sends an HTTPS request.
The Zscaler service intercepts the HTTPS request. Through a separate SSL/TLS tunnel, the service sends its own HTTPS request to the destination server and conducts SSL/TLS negotiations.
The destination server sends the Zscaler service its certificate with its public key.
The Zscaler service and destination server complete the SSL/TLS handshake. The application data and subsequent messages are sent through the SSL/TLS tunnel.

The Zscaler service conducts SSL/TLS negotiations with the user’s browser. It sends the browser the Zscaler intermediate certificate or your organization’s custom intermediate root, as well as a server certificate signed by the Zscaler intermediate Certificate Authority (CA). The browser validates the certificate chain in the browser's certificate store. To learn more, see Choosing the CA Certificate for SSL/TLS Inspection.

blocks.text: Zscaler issued certificates (leaf or short-lived issuing CA) contain a CRL Distribution Point (CRLDP) hosted by Zscaler that provides a mechanism for certification revocation.
